page.overview:
Who is Balrog?

Balrog, known as in Japan or known internationally as Boxer, is a video game character from the Street Fighter series, first appearing as a non-playable boss in Street Fighter II before becoming playable in its update, Street Fighter II: Champion Edition. He is a greedy American boxer who loves booze, gambling and ladies. He is also a personal bodyguard to M. Bison.

Designed by "Pigmon-san" and Akira "Akiman" Yasuda, the 4th original character concept for a early prototype boxer began in an early 1988 character pitch, starting out as a Caucasian named Dick Jumpsey who is based on both American professional boxer Jack Dempsey as well as American actor and fellow professional boxer Mickey Rourke. Jumpsey is a superstar as both an actor and athlete (a character bio later passed down to Fei-Long), his planned plot states that he enters the tournament to publicize his next movie. Due to being a pugilist, Jumpsey's controls consists of both "jabbing" and "hooking" instead of punching and kicking unlike the rest of the street fighters, what makes his style of boxing so unique is his heavy punches, powerful blocking techniques, and his signature special move called the Holy Rope Storm and his weakness is getting hit in his back while turning around to charge a strong jab, a weakness that would be passed onto Balrog solely in The World Warrior, but the Turn Punch would be given to Balrog in every game he appears in.

The wrestler Zangief (under the name "Vodka Golbalsky" during development) was originally written as the professional-ring fighter who does not follow the rules or what to do while making his opponents completely unable to recover, and then makes easy money by doing underground brawling. These traits were later given to Balrog.

Another inspiration may include Leon Spinks, the undisputed world heavyweight champion of 1978 who won the title against Muhammad Ali, and whose 1980s undisputed heavyweight champion young brother Michael Spinks faced off against Mike Tyson in 1988 in his only loss and last match of his career. Notably, Leon Spinks would also turn to competing in boxer versus wrestler matches in New Japan Pro Wrestling during the 1980s, including a famous loss by submission to Antonio Inoki, and into the 1990s, would compete in Frontier Martial-Arts Wrestling, which he would win the title of world champion by 1992.
